explanations.explanation: Hospitality to strangers, yes. The writer says that by doing it “some people have entertained angels without knowing it.” Nobody wore a name tag, friend. I'd be wiping down every counter in my bakery just in case.

The writer doesn't mention praying in the temple here. He says, “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it.” So the angel guests came through welcoming strangers. It's a fair guess, but the verse points to the open door.

Keeping the Sabbath isn't what this verse is talking about. The writer says some people entertained angels without knowing it, and he ties that to showing hospitality to strangers. So the secret is in how you treat the person at your door. I'd keep a spare cookie handy, just in case.

explanations.answer: As if you were bound with them
explanations.explanation: That's the line: “Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them…” He doesn't say to remember them from a distance. I think he means to feel it like it's happening to you. And he adds the mistreated too, “as if you were suffering with them.”

explanations.answer: As if you were their judge
explanations.explanation: The writer never puts the reader in the judge's seat. He says, “Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them…” So the picture is standing right beside them, not above them. I think that's a much kinder place to stand.

explanations.answer: As if you were their guard
explanations.explanation: No guard in this verse, friend. The writer says to remember those in prison “as if you were bound with them…” That means being with them in their chains, not watching over the door. He says the same about those who are mistreated, as if you were suffering with them.
The writer says it the other way around. He says, “Marriage should be honored by all…” That word is all, not only the people wearing rings. So everybody is asked to honor it.

False is right. The writer says, “Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled…” He doesn't limit it to the married. He adds that God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.

explanations.answer: God has said He will never leave them
explanations.explanation: This is the reason the writer gives. He says to be content with what you have, “for God has said: ‘Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.’” The cookie jar may run low, friend, but that promise doesn't. Having God with you is a lot of treasure.

explanations.answer: Money always runs out in the end
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't give that reason. He says to be content with what you have, “for God has said: ‘Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.’” So contentment rests on God staying with you. A fat wallet isn't part of the argument.

explanations.answer: Their reward is coming very soon
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't mention a reward coming soon here. His reason is what God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.” That's what lets a person be content with what they have. The promise is the whole reason.

True. Right after the promise, the writer says, “So we say with confidence: ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?’” The confidence comes from God staying close. And that question at the end makes me stand up a little taller.

It's true, friend. Right after “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you,” the writer says, “So we say with confidence: ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?’” Notice the word so. The promise comes first, and the confidence follows from it.

Imitate is it. The writer says to remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you, consider the outcome of their way of life, and “imitate their faith.” Notice he says their faith, not their haircuts. Follow the part that counts.

Question isn't the word. The writer says, “Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith.” These are the leaders who spoke the word of God to them. So he's pointing the readers to follow that faith.

The writer says the opposite of forget. He opens the verse with “Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you.” Then he says to consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith. So keep them in mind, friend.
Teachings, right. The writer says, “Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings…” Carried away sounds like getting swept off by a current to me. He wants their hearts to stay put.

Dreams aren't in this verse. The writer says, “Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings…” So the danger is teachings that don't match what they've heard. Sleep as many dreams as you like, friend.

No storms here, though that would be dramatic. The writer says, “Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings…” The thing that can carry them off is teaching, not weather. I think that's the quieter danger.

Grace is right. The writer says, “…it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them.” The foods didn't do those folks any good. Grace is what holds the heart up.

Effort isn't the word. The writer says, “…it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them.” So the heart gets its strength from grace. Hard work has its place, but it's not what this verse names.

Riches aren't named in this verse. The writer says it's good for the heart to be strengthened “by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them.” Grace is the strength-giver. It's a free gift, so it doesn't come with a price tag.

Outside the city gate is it. The writer says, “And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.” That matches the animal bodies burned outside the camp in the verse before. He's connecting the two.

The Holy Place is where the high priest brings the blood of animals, according to the verse before. But Jesus suffered somewhere else. The writer says, “And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate…” The word also ties Him to the bodies burned outside the camp.

The Jordan isn't mentioned in this passage. The writer says, “And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.” That's the place he names. It's outside, not beside a river.
The disgrace He bore, yes. The writer says, “Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore.” It's not a comfortable invitation. But it's an invitation to go to Jesus.
The blood isn't what the writer says we carry. Jesus sanctifies the people by His own blood in the verse before. What we bear is “the disgrace He bore.” So we go to Him outside the camp with that.
Tablets aren't in this passage at all. The writer says, “Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore.” That's what we carry. We leave the luggage behind, friend.

The writer says the opposite. He says, “For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.” So believers don't have a permanent city here. They're looking ahead.

False is right. The writer says, “For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.” So no permanent city here, but one is coming. That's a good thing to know when the moving boxes pile up.

Praise is it. The writer says, “Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.” Lips that confess His name are what make the fruit. Nothing to carry, nothing to count.

Silver isn't what he names. The writer says, “…let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.” So the offering comes from lips, not a purse. Your pockets can stay put.

Grain isn't in this verse. The writer says, “Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.” Praise is what he names, and continually is how often. No measuring cups needed.

explanations.answer: Doing good and sharing with others
explanations.explanation: Right. The writer says, “And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.” So doing good and sharing both count as sacrifices. I'll hand out a few extra cookies today, friend.

Fasting and all-night praying aren't named here. The writer says, “And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.” The sacrifices he names are doing good and sharing. Good things to do on an ordinary Tuesday.

No temple gifts in this verse. The writer says, “And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.” He names doing good and sharing. Those are the sacrifices that please God.
Give an account, right. The writer says leaders “watch over your souls as those who must give an account.” That's a serious job. I'd say they deserve our patience, friend.
Earning trust isn't what the writer says. He says leaders “watch over your souls as those who must give an account.” So the weight on them is giving an account. Trust isn't the word he uses.
Praise isn't the point in this verse. The writer says leaders “watch over your souls as those who must give an account.” That's what they must do. Applause isn't part of the job description.
True. The writer says, “…allow them to lead with joy and not with grief, for that would be of no advantage to you.” So grief doesn't help the people. A joyful leader is a gift to everybody.

It's true, friend. The writer says, “…allow them to lead with joy and not with grief, for that would be of no advantage to you.” So leading with grief does the people no good. That's his reason to let leaders lead with joy.

explanations.answer: That he may be restored to them soon
explanations.explanation: That's it. The writer says, “And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon.” The word especially tells me this one matters to him. I think he misses them.

explanations.answer: That his letter will reach every church
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't ask for that. He says, “And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon.” So his special request is about being restored to them. It's more personal than a mailing list.

explanations.answer: That his enemies will be stopped
explanations.explanation: Enemies aren't mentioned in this verse. The writer says, “And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon.” So he asks them to pray that he'll be back with them. I think it's a very human request.

explanations.answer: The blood of the eternal covenant
explanations.explanation: Right. The writer says God “through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep.” That's a big line to pack into one sentence. It's worth reading twice.

The writer doesn't name the prayers of the disciples here. He says God brought back Jesus from the dead “through the blood of the eternal covenant.” So that's the something. It's a covenant that lasts forever.

Moses and the law aren't in this verse. The writer says God brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus “through the blood of the eternal covenant.” That's the something he names. And he calls Jesus the great Shepherd of the sheep.
Will, yes. The writer says, “…equip you with every good thing to do His will.” God does the equipping, and we get to do the doing. That takes a lot of pressure off, friend.
Miracles aren't in this verse. The writer says, “…equip you with every good thing to do His will.” What God equips us to do is His will. I'd say that's the bigger job.
Judgments aren't the word. The writer says, “…equip you with every good thing to do His will.” So the blessing is about doing His will. It's a warm thing to say at the end of a letter.

The writer says the opposite. He says, “I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly.” So he calls it brief. I'd say that's generous, friend, but it's his word.

False is right. The writer says, “I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly.” He says he wrote briefly, not at length. So he's asking them to bear with it.
Released, yes. The writer says, “Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released.” That's good news to pass along. Timothy is the brother he's talking about.
It's the other direction, friend. The writer says, “Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released.” So Timothy is free, not arrested. Good news to carry down the line.

Sailing isn't in the writer's news. He says, “Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released.” Italy only comes up later, when he says, “Those from Italy send you greetings.” So the news about Timothy is that he's been released.
True. The writer says, “If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you.” So the plan depends on Timothy arriving soon. I think that's a nice way to end a letter, with a visit coming.
It's true, friend. The writer says, “If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you.” So he plans to come along with Timothy. That's if Timothy arrives soon.
